ideas.title: Ask how similar projects actually went
ideas.idea:
When you plan something, you naturally look at its details: the steps, the people, the obstacles you can foresee. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky called this the inside view, and it is reliably too optimistic, because it can only count the problems you can imagine. The outside view does the opposite. You ignore the particulars at first and ask what happened to similar projects in the past: how long did they take, what did they cost, how many never finished? Start from that record, then adjust for what is genuinely different about your case.

Kahneman's own example is a school curriculum he helped design in Israel. Everyone on the team, including him, guessed about two years. When he finally asked a colleague with experience of similar projects, the honest answer was far gloomier. It took eight. The unsettling part is that he already had the information; it just never occurred to anyone to use it until asked.
ideas.deep_dive:
The distinction comes from Kahneman and Tversky's work in the 1970s on forecasting and the planning fallacy. Kahneman tells the curriculum story in Thinking, Fast and Slow and in a McKinsey Quarterly interview. After about a year of work, each team member wrote down how long a complete draft would take. The guesses ran from 18 to 30 months. Then Kahneman asked Seymour Fox, the curriculum expert on the team, to recall similar teams at the same stage. The real project took eight, and the ministry had lost interest by the time it was done.

The Danish planning scholar Bent Flyvbjerg turned this into a working method, reference class forecasting. You pick a class of comparable past projects, build a distribution of their outcomes (for example cost overrun), and place your project within it. The more your project resembles the class, the more weight the class deserves. Flyvbjerg's approach was taken up in UK appraisal guidance in the early 2000s, which gave planners standard percentage uplifts for optimism bias.

It has limits. A reference class is only as good as its data, and choosing it is a judgement: a bridge may belong with bridges, tunnels or all megaprojects, and each gives a different answer. Truly novel projects have no good class. And the method corrects the numbers, not the incentives; if sponsors gain from low estimates, they may simply argue about which class applies. Used well, it is a starting point for a harder conversation, not a final answer.

examples.title: The curriculum that took eight years
examples.text: In the 1970s Kahneman worked with a team, including the Hebrew University dean Seymour Fox, on a decision-making curriculum for Israeli schools. A year in, members estimated 18 to 30 months to a full draft. Asked about comparable teams, Fox said many never finished and the rest took seven to ten years. Kahneman says the team noted this and carried on regardless. The textbook took eight years and, by then, the ministry's enthusiasm had faded and it was not used. The case shows the inside view winning even when the outside view was sitting in the room.

examples.title: HM Treasury's optimism bias uplifts
examples.text: The UK Treasury's Green Book acknowledges that appraisers are systematically over-optimistic. Supplementary guidance, based on a 2002 Mott MacDonald review of past public projects, sets upper-bound capital cost uplifts by type: 24 per cent for standard buildings, 44 per cent for standard civil engineering, 51 per cent for non-standard buildings and 66 per cent for non-standard civil engineering. Planners start from these figures and may reduce them only where they can show that specific risks have been managed. The figures reflect average historic overruns at outline business case stage, so earlier stages may need more.

examples.title: Edinburgh trams, a method meeting reality
examples.text: In 2004 Flyvbjerg and the consultancy Cowi built a reference class of 46 rail projects with the UK Department for Transport; Edinburgh Tram Line 2 was an early practical use of the method. Later the Edinburgh Tram Inquiry heard Flyvbjerg's evidence that the main tram contract was let with an optimism bias allowance of zero per cent, on the grounds that all risks were known. The line from the airport to Newhaven was first budgeted at £545 million; the shorter airport to York Place line that opened in 2014 had a best-estimate cost of £835.7 million. The council disputed his framing.

examples.title: The Olympics as a reference class
examples.text: A 2016 Oxford study by Flyvbjerg and colleagues looked at cost data for 19 of the 30 Summer and Winter Games held since 1960. It found an average overrun of 156 per cent in real terms, the highest of any megaproject type they had studied. For comparison, reported averages for roads were around 20 per cent, rail 45 per cent and IT projects 107 per cent. The authors recommend that future host cities base their budgets on previous Games' actual costs rather than on a bottom-up estimate of their own bid.

images.caption: Daniel Kahneman, whose curriculum-planning story is the classic illustration of the inside view versus the outside view.
images.credit: nrkbeta / CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

why: Kahneman's anecdote is one team's story told from memory, but Flyvbjerg's data on large infrastructure projects is extensive and consistent: overruns are the norm, not the exception.
UK government guidance has used reference-class uplifts since the early 2000s, though the Edinburgh trams show that having the method does not guarantee it is applied.
The main limit is choosing the reference class, and novel projects may have no good one.
ideas.try_this: Think of something you are planning with a deadline. Before estimating it, list three similar things you or others have done and how long each actually took. Does your usual estimate survive that comparison?

ideas.title: Imagine the plan failed, then explain why
ideas.idea: A premortem asks a team to do something that feels slightly perverse: before a project starts, imagine it is a year later and the project has failed completely, then write down why. The psychologist Gary Klein proposed the technique in the Harvard Business Review in 2007, as a counterweight to the optimism and quiet self-censorship that creep into planning meetings. Once a plan has momentum, doubting it feels disloyal, so people with reservations stay silent. The premortem changes the job. Failure is treated as a given, so naming a weakness is no longer an attack on the plan; it is the task. Because the failure is imagined as already having happened, people also tend to come up with more concrete, specific causes than when they are asked what might go wrong. Someone who suspects a weakness finally has permission to say so, while fixing it is still cheap.
ideas.deep_dive:
Klein built the idea on an older finding. In 1989 the psychologists Deborah Mitchell, Jay Russo and Nancy Pennington reported in the Journal of Behavioral Decision Making that people asked to explain an event as if it had already happened ("prospective hindsight") generated roughly 30 per cent more reasons than people asked to consider what might happen. Klein took that effect and turned it into a short group exercise: describe the plan, ask everyone to imagine it has failed, give them a few minutes to write down every reason they can think of, then go round the room collecting one reason at a time until the list is exhausted. The team then revises the plan to deal with the most serious items.

It is worth being precise about what the evidence shows. The 30 per cent figure measured the number of reasons produced, not how accurate or important they were, so claims that premortems find 30 per cent more of the real risks go further than the study. The most direct test of the technique itself, by Veinott, Klein and Wiggins in 2010, was a small experiment with students and found that the premortem lowered confidence in a plan more than a standard critique or a pros-and-cons list. Lower confidence is not the same as better outcomes, and independent research on premortems is thin.

Its value is therefore best understood as social as much as cognitive: it makes dissent safe and routine. It works best before commitment, when the plan can still change. It does little if a decision has already been made for other reasons.

examples.title: The algorithm that would not fit on laptops
examples.text: In his 2007 Harvard Business Review article, Klein described a premortem on a project to put advanced algorithms into the hands of air-campaign planners. One team member had said nothing throughout the kickoff. When asked to explain a future failure, he pointed out that one of the algorithms would not run quickly enough on the laptops used in the field. The developers already knew of a shortcut but had been reluctant to mention it. It was substituted into the plan, and the project went on to succeed. The exercise had not produced new analysis so much as given someone permission to speak.

examples.title: Health-care teams plan for failure in advance
examples.text: The US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality includes a premortem in its CUSP patient-safety programme for hospital units. The facilitator's script asks the team to imagine it is two years on and, despite everyone's efforts, the programme has failed on their unit. People work alone for about ten minutes, then share one reason each, going round the room until none remain. The team ranks the list and addresses the top two or three concerns, then revisits it during the programme. It is a deliberate, institutional use of Klein's method, built into a standard toolkit.

examples.title: Does imagining failure lower confidence?
examples.text: In 2010 Elizabeth Veinott, Gary Klein and Sarah Wiggins tested the technique on 178 university students who assessed a university's plan for handling an H1N1 outbreak. Different groups used a standard critique, a pros-and-cons list, a cons-only list or a premortem, in which they imagined the plan had failed and wrote down why. Confidence in the plan fell most in the premortem group, by about twice as much as with the pros-and-cons or cons-only approaches, according to summaries of the paper. The study was small and used students, but it is the main experimental support for the premortem itself.

why: The underlying effect (more reasons generated under prospective hindsight) comes from a 1989 peer-reviewed study, but it counted reasons, not their quality.
Direct evidence for the premortem is limited to small studies such as Veinott and colleagues (2010, 178 students); the field accounts are largely Klein's own.
It helps most before a plan is locked in; it is weaker where the decision has effectively been made.
ideas.try_this: Pick a plan you are about to commit to this week. Spend five minutes writing, as if it had already happened, the reasons it failed. Which reason would you least like to say aloud, and what is the cheapest way to deal with it now?

ideas.title: Peto's paradox: why giants rarely get cancer
ideas.idea: Every cell division carries a small chance of a cancer-causing mutation. So an animal with a thousand times more cells, living many times longer, ought to be far more likely to develop cancer. Yet across species it does not work that way. Whales and elephants are not riddled with tumours, and a mouse is not safer than a human. This puzzle is called Peto's paradox, after the epidemiologist Richard Peto, who noticed it in the 1970s. The most likely answer is that evolution has repeatedly strengthened cancer defences in big, long-lived animals, because without them they would never have reached that size. Elephants are the best-studied case: they carry around 20 copies of TP53, a gene that tells damaged cells to die rather than divide. A human has one. The explanation is still argued over, but it shows cancer is not just bad luck accumulating: it is a risk that bodies are built to manage.
ideas.deep_dive:
Peto's point, made in the 1970s, came from comparing mice and people. A human has roughly a thousand times more cells than a mouse and lives about thirty times longer, so if cancer simply tracked the number of cell divisions, humans would get it constantly. In practice lifetime cancer rates are similar in the two species. Peto's observation was about mice and humans; the broader claim is that this holds across species. A 2022 analysis in Nature by Orsolya Vincze and colleagues, using records for more than 100,000 zoo animals from 191 species, found that cancer incidence was independent of body size and adult life expectancy.

The natural explanation is natural selection. An animal that grows to four tonnes without strong tumour suppression would tend not to survive to breed, so the lineages that became large are the ones that also evolved extra protection. In elephants, two teams reported in 2015 and 2016 that the genome has about 20 copies of TP53 (one full gene and 19 retrogenes, which are copies made from the gene's messenger RNA). Elephant cells in the JAMA study died more readily after DNA damage than human cells did. Other animals appear to have taken different routes. The bowhead whale, which may live beyond 200 years, shows changes in DNA repair genes rather than extra TP53.

There are limits. The TP53 evidence is correlational and the cell experiments used small samples. A 2022 re-evaluation by Leonard Nunney questioned how the retrogenes work, and a 2025 paper argued there is no clear evidence for the paradox in land vertebrates at all. The sensible reading is that the paradox is a useful question, not a settled law.

examples.title: Elephant cells and the extra TP53 copies
examples.text: In 2015 a team led by Joshua Schiffman at the University of Utah, with Carlo Maley's group, published a study in JAMA. From zoo records they estimated that about 4.8 per cent of elephants die of cancer, against 11 to 25 per cent of humans. They found at least 20 copies of TP53 in African elephants. After radiation damage, elephant white blood cells died by apoptosis at a much higher rate, about 14.6 per cent, than human control cells at about 7.2 per cent. The lab groups were small, with eight elephants, so the authors were cautious about what it proves.

examples.title: The bowhead whale genome
examples.text: In 2015 Joao Pedro de Magalhaes's group at Liverpool and colleagues published the first bowhead whale genome in Cell Reports. Bowheads, which are thought to live for over 200 years, are huge and Arctic. The team found changes in genes involved in DNA repair, cell cycle control and ageing, including mutations in ERCC1 and duplications of PCNA. These are candidate explanations only. Nobody has yet shown that those variants are what protects the whales, but the work suggests that a different animal has found a different solution from the elephant.

examples.title: A hundred thousand zoo animals
examples.text: Rather than rely on a few famous species, Vincze and colleagues in 2022 drew on veterinary records from zoos worldwide. They covered more than 100,000 animals from 191 mammal species. They found that species of greater size, or with longer lives, did not get cancer more often. This is the sort of broad check Peto's idea needed. It is also why later authors dispute it: a 2025 paper using other data argued that the paradox is not supported in land vertebrates, so the debate is live.

images.credit: NOAA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: African bush elephants, whose genome holds around 20 copies of the TP53 tumour suppressor gene.

why: Two independent 2015-16 genetic studies (Abegglen et al. in JAMA; Sulak et al. in eLife) found about 20 TP53 copies in elephants, and a 2022 Nature study of 191 species supports the broader pattern.
Caveats: the cell experiments used few animals, the retrogene mechanism is debated, and some later analyses dispute the paradox itself in land vertebrates.
ideas.try_this: Think of one risk in your own work that you assume grows in proportion to size or time. What defences has it quietly built up that make the simple multiplication wrong?

ideas.title: Were we ever meant to sleep once?
ideas.idea:
The idea that a good night is eight unbroken hours may be a recent habit rather than a biological rule. The historian Roger Ekirch argues that in pre-industrial Britain and much of Europe, people commonly slept in two parts: a "first sleep" soon after dark, an hour or two awake, then a "second sleep" until morning. The waking spell was ordinary, not a problem. People prayed, talked, tended the fire, checked animals or simply lay thinking. In 1992 the psychiatrist Thomas Wehr gave volunteers long, dark winter-style nights and found that their sleep split in a similar way.

The useful point is not that we should copy the Middle Ages. It is that waking in the small hours may not always be a malfunction, and that the worry about it can make it worse. The caveat matters too: the historical reading is disputed, and studies of people living without electricity show a more mixed picture than the tidy story suggests.
ideas.deep_dive:
Ekirch first met the pattern in a 1697 legal record that mentioned a person's "first sleep". He kept looking and, in his 2001 paper "Sleep We Have Lost" and his 2005 book At Day's Close, set out references to first and second sleep in diaries, court records, medical texts, prayer books and literature, going back as far as Homer's Odyssey. Counts vary between accounts, from several hundred to over two thousand across a dozen languages, so treat any single number with care. He argues that the second sleep shrank from the late seventeenth century onwards as artificial light spread, and that consolidated sleep was the norm by the early nineteenth century.

The laboratory evidence comes from Thomas Wehr at the US National Institute of Mental Health. In a 1992 paper, "In short photoperiods, human sleep is biphasic", healthy volunteers were moved from a 16-hour day to a 10-hour one, so they had 14 hours of darkness. Their sleep lengthened and usually divided into two bouts of several hours with a waking interval of one to three hours. Wehr suggested this might reflect an older, more natural pattern. Accounts differ on the exact number of men and the length of the study, so I have not quoted them here.

The limits are real. In 2023 the historian Niall Boyce argued in Medical History that the phrases "first sleep" and "second sleep" were not fixed in meaning, and that the evidence is ambiguous. Ekirch replied that this reading is selective. The sleep scientist Jerome Siegel and colleagues found no segmented sleep in three hunter-gatherer groups. Wehr's volunteers were also in an artificial setting. A fair summary is that segmented sleep was probably common in some places and periods, but not proven to be universal or "natural".

examples.title: Wehr's long nights at the NIH
examples.text: In the early 1990s Thomas Wehr and colleagues at the US National Institute of Mental Health took healthy volunteers from a normal 16-hour day to a 10-hour day, leaving 14 hours of darkness. After an initial period of catching up on sleep, their nights tended to split into two symmetrical bouts of several hours, with one to three hours of quiet wakefulness between them. The result appeared in 1992. It does not prove that this is humanity's default, but it shows that, given long dark nights and little to do, the body can settle into two sleeps.

examples.title: A rural village in Madagascar
examples.text: In a 2017 paper in the American Journal of Human Biology, David Samson and colleagues studied 21 adults in a small farming community in Madagascar with no electricity. They tracked 292 days of sleep with wrist monitors, and recorded the first full polysomnography from a traditional population. Sleep was segmented, which fits the historical pattern, and daytime napping appeared on 88 per cent of days. But sleep was also shorter and poorer than in industrial comparison groups, with 162 minutes awake after sleep onset on average. Segmented does not mean restful.

examples.title: Hadza, San and Tsimane: a counterpoint
examples.text: In 2015, Gandhi Yetish and colleagues reported on sleep in three societies without electricity: the Hadza of Tanzania, the San of Namibia and the Tsimane of Bolivia. Average sleep was about 6.4 hours, people fell asleep around three hours after sunset, and napping was rare. The authors did not describe a two-part night. Ekirch has questioned how far these findings undercut his case, and Siegel has argued that such data outweigh anecdotes in old records. The disagreement is why the idea should be held loosely.

images.caption: An 1893 furniture-history illustration of a French medieval bedroom, the kind of shared, dim space in which a night might be broken into two sleeps.
images.credit: Via Wikimedia Commons (author and licence on the file page)

why: Evidence is strongest for the documentary record in Britain and Ireland, where Ekirch found many references to a first and second sleep, and for Wehr's small laboratory study.
Caveats: Boyce (2023) argues the historical wording is ambiguous, and a 2015 study of three hunter-gatherer groups found single-block sleep. Madagascar data show segmentation but also poor sleep.
It is not medical advice. If broken sleep distresses you, speak to a doctor.
ideas.try_this: If you wake in the night, try treating it as a quiet interval rather than a failure: no clock-checking, dim light, a few calm minutes, and notice whether the worry about it shrinks.

ideas.title: Fresh starts: why Mondays feel like beginnings
ideas.idea: People are more likely to start something new when the calendar offers a clean break. Hengchen Dai, Katy Milkman and Jason Riis call this the fresh start effect. Dates such as the first day of a week, a month, a semester or a year, or a birthday, mark a boundary between the person you were and the person you plan to be. Past slips get filed under the old period, which makes a new attempt feel more believable. In their 2014 study, Google searches for 'diet', visits to a university gym and public commitments to goals all rose after these landmarks, and not only in January. The practical point is that motivation is not spread evenly through the year. It clusters around moments that feel like beginnings, and those moments can be borrowed. A Monday, the first of the month or your own birthday can do the job, though a burst of enthusiasm does not guarantee the habit lasts.
ideas.deep_dive:
Dai, Milkman and Riis published 'The Fresh Start Effect: Temporal Landmarks Motivate Aspirational Behavior' in Management Science in 2014. They combined three sets of archival data: Google search volume for the word 'diet', attendance records from a university gym, and goal commitments made on the website stickK. In each, the behaviour rose after landmarks such as the start of a week, month, year or semester, or a birthday. The authors' explanation is a kind of mental accounting. Landmarks cut time into new periods and push past failings into a closed one, and they also lift attention from daily detail to the bigger picture.

The strongest causal test came later. In 2021, Beshears, Dai, Milkman and Benartzi reported a randomised field experiment with 6,082 university employees, published in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes. Mailings that tied a future savings increase to a fresh start, such as a birthday or the first day of spring, made people more likely to choose it. Mailings tied to Thanksgiving or Valentine's Day, which are not usually seen as beginnings, did not help.

There are limits. The 2014 data are observational, so other explanations cannot be fully excluded; one blogger has suggested regression to the mean, which is a secondary opinion rather than a formal rebuttal. I found no independent replication, and the later field experiment came from the same research group. Fresh starts also do not always help: experiments summarised by Psychology Today in 2018 found that a reset can aid performance after failure but hurt it after success. And a surge of motivation at the start says little about whether the habit survives the second week.

examples.title: Birthday-framed savings letters at a university
examples.text: In the Beshears, Dai, Milkman and Benartzi experiment, 6,082 university employees received mailings offering a choice: raise their savings-plan contributions now, or at a later point. For some, the later point was framed as a fresh start, such as the recipient's next birthday or the first day of spring. Those mailings made people more likely to choose the future increase, without reducing the number choosing an immediate one. Coverage of the study reports roughly 25% more cumulative contributions over the following eight months than from other mailings. Mailings tied to Thanksgiving or Valentine's Day had no such effect.

examples.title: Diet searches, gym visits and stickK goals
examples.text: Dai, Milkman and Riis studied what people did without being prompted. Searches for 'diet' rose around New Year, but also at the start of the week, the start of the month and after national holidays. At a university gym, card-reader records showed attendance rising around landmarks such as the start of a week or semester and after a birthday. Commitments on the goal-setting site stickK followed a similar pattern. Nobody was nudged: the clean-break pattern simply showed up in ordinary behaviour, which is why the finding reaches well beyond New Year resolutions.

examples.title: When wiping the slate backfires
examples.text: Four experiments, summarised by Psychology Today in 2018, tested what happens when a fresh start is imposed rather than chosen. In the first, participants were paid per correct word in a word game, and one group had their last five rounds scored from zero. The reported conclusion was that a reset helps after a failure but can make performance worse when the earlier results were good. The everyday lesson is that a clean slate suits a bad run, not a good one. The summary does not name the authors, so treat the details as secondary.

why: The 2014 paper draws on three archival datasets (Google searches, a university gym, stickK), and a 2021 randomised field experiment with 6,082 university employees supports it.
Caveat: the first evidence is observational, I found no independent replication, and the later experiment came from the same group.
A fresh start can lift the first step without making the habit last, and resets can hurt after success.
ideas.try_this: Pick one thing you keep putting off and attach it to the next landmark, such as the first of next month, a Monday or your birthday. Then ask honestly whether the landmark is doing real work, or whether you could simply start today.

ideas.title: You understand less than you think
ideas.idea:
Ask yourself how well you understand a zip. Most people say fairly well. Now write out, step by step, how it actually works. Somewhere around the second sentence you notice the gap: you know what a zip does, not how it does it. That sudden drop in confidence is the illusion of explanatory depth, named by Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil at Yale in 2002.

The illusion appears because familiar things feel understood. You can use a zip, a toilet or a bicycle without fault, and the ease of use, plus the fact that you can see the parts, is mistaken for knowing the mechanism. The feeling of understanding is cheap, and it only gets tested when you are made to explain.

The practical lesson is a test, not a scolding: before you trust a feeling of understanding, try to explain the thing from start to finish, out loud or on paper.
ideas.deep_dive:
Rozenblit and Keil, writing in Cognitive Science in 2002, asked participants to rate how well they understood everyday devices such as zips, flush toilets, piano keys and cylinder locks. They then asked them to write detailed explanations, gave them a correct account, and asked them to rate themselves again. Ratings fell, often sharply. The drop was much smaller for other kinds of knowledge, such as facts (the capital of a country) or procedures (how to bake a cake), where people can tell more easily whether they know the answer. It persisted in other groups of people, and warning people in advance that they would have to explain reduced it but did not remove it.

The likely mechanism is that we confuse levels of understanding. We know what a device is for, what it looks like and how to operate it, and that high-level knowledge feels like depth. Because the world itself holds much of the detail, we rarely need to carry it in our heads, so we rarely find out that it is missing.

The idea was extended to politics. In 2013 Philip Fernbach, Todd Rogers, Craig Fox and Steven Sloman found that asking people to explain how a policy would work, rather than why they favoured it, lowered their confidence and moderated their stated views.

Here honesty matters. The core finding, that explaining lowers confidence in your understanding, has replicated repeatedly. The political moderation effect has not: a preregistered replication by Crawford and Ruscio in 2021 found no significant moderation, and Sloman and Vives (2022) found it only for issues argued on consequences, not on deeply held values.

examples.title: Explaining policies, not defending them
examples.text: In the 2013 experiments reported in Psychological Science, Fernbach and colleagues asked US participants to rate their understanding of policies such as cap-and-trade or a flat tax. Some then wrote a step-by-step account of how the policy would produce its effects. Their confidence in their own understanding fell, and their attitudes became more moderate. Others merely listed reasons for their view and showed no such change. In a further experiment, people who had explained a policy gave less money to related advocacy groups. The authors argued that the confidence behind polarised views partly rests on shallow causal models.

examples.title: Strong opponents of GM food
examples.text: In a 2019 study in Nature Human Behaviour, Fernbach and colleagues surveyed over 2,000 adults in the United States, France and Germany. The more strongly people opposed genetically modified food, the better they thought they understood it, yet the worse they scored on a test of actual science and genetics knowledge. The same pattern appeared for gene therapy but not for climate change denial, which the authors linked to its stronger political polarisation. They suggested that education may work only after people first notice the limits of what they know.

examples.title: The toilet and the zip, again
examples.text: Fernbach, co-author of The Knowledge Illusion, opens his TEDxMileHigh talk on this subject with a diagram of a toilet and asks the audience whether they could explain how it works. The point matches the original 2002 experiment, where flush toilets and zips were among the items that people rated as well understood and then struggled to describe. It is a test anyone can run at home: try describing, without looking, what happens inside the cistern when you press the handle and why the water stops.

examples.title: Replications that tested the political claim
examples.text: Science has also applied the idea to itself. In 2021 Crawford and Ruscio ran a preregistered replication of the policy-explanation experiment and found that asking people to explain complex policies did not significantly increase moderation. In 2022 Sloman and Vives, with more current issues, found that explanation lowered both understanding and extremity only for consequence-based issues, not for issues tied to protected values. The humility effect held up, while the political effect proved narrower than first claimed.

why: The central effect, that explaining a mechanism lowers your confidence in your understanding, has been replicated several times, in the original Yale studies and later by other groups.
The claim that explaining policies makes people more moderate is much shakier: a preregistered 2021 replication did not find it, and a 2022 study found it only for consequence-based issues.
It applies to mechanisms and causal stories, not to facts or procedures, and it says nothing about who is right on any issue.
ideas.try_this: Pick something you use daily, such as a zip, a toilet or a bicycle gear, and rate your understanding from 1 to 7. Then explain how it works, step by step, on paper. Re-rate yourself, and notice which step you could not fill in.

ideas.title: Evil can come from not imagining others
ideas.idea:
Hannah Arendt coined 'the banality of evil' to describe something unsettling: terrible acts do not need a monster to carry them out. Reporting on the 1961 trial of Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem, she expected a fanatic and found a man who spoke almost entirely in stock phrases and officialese. In her view the problem was not stupidity but thoughtlessness: an inability to stop and think what his actions meant for the people on the receiving end. She tied it to speech: his failure to say anything fresh seemed linked to his failure to think from anyone else's standpoint.

The idea travels well because it describes a habit rather than a type of person. Whenever we hide behind procedure, jargon or 'that's just the process', we are practising a mild version of it. Arendt did not say Eichmann was innocent, or that evil is dull. She said that refusing to imagine another person's position can pave the way for harm.
ideas.deep_dive:
Arendt attended the trial as a reporter for The New Yorker, and the resulting book, Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil, appeared in 1963. By 'banality' she meant that his motives looked shallow, not that his crimes were trivial. She held him fully responsible and supported his execution. What struck her was his reliance on clichés and bureaucratic language, which she read as a sign that he was not engaging with reality as other people experienced it.

Later she developed this into a theory of thinking. Drawing on Kant's 'enlarged mentality', she meant the practice of considering a matter from the position of others. This is not empathy, which involves sharing feelings. It is a discipline of reasoning, and in her later essay 'Thinking and Moral Considerations' (1971) she asked whether the habit of internal dialogue works as a brake on wrongdoing.

The idea has been seriously challenged. Bettina Stangneth's Eichmann Before Jerusalem (2011) drew on interviews Eichmann gave in Argentina in the 1950s, in which he spoke with pride about his part in the killings and showed a committed ideological antisemitism. Her argument, and that of other critics, is that Arendt was taken in by a courtroom performance. Others reply that critics misread Arendt, who never claimed he was a mere order-follower, and that her concept describes how ordinary people take part in evil rather than his biography. Both points are worth holding. The safest use of the idea is as a warning about unexamined routine, not as a verdict on Eichmann.

examples.title: Milgram, Arendt and a challenge from St Andrews
examples.text: Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments were often read alongside Arendt: he proposed that people slip into an 'agentic state' and focus on following instructions. Alex Haslam and Stephen Reicher at St Andrews reviewed the evidence and argued otherwise. Across Milgram's variants, the share of people going to the top voltage ranged from 0% to nearly 100%, which an automatic state of obedience struggles to explain. They concluded that many participants identified with the scientific project and believed they were doing right. Their research challenges Arendt's picture, so it is a useful test of the idea rather than a confirmation of it.

examples.title: A Post Office culture that closed its mind
examples.text: In the Post Office Horizon inquiry, closing submissions for subpostmasters were made by Edward Henry KC. He argued that the Post Office's culture, not only the faulty software, destroyed lives, and that managers 'closed their minds and closed ranks around the system'. Alan Davies, a former communications head, told the inquiry that 'we really believed we were doing the right things' and that some of his old emails now looked 'ludicrous'. The sources do not invoke Arendt, but the pattern, conviction without imagining the person on the other end, is the kind of failure she described.

examples.title: Stangneth tests the thesis against Eichmann's own words
examples.text: Bettina Stangneth's Eichmann Before Jerusalem used material from interviews that Eichmann gave to the Dutch journalist Willem Sassen in Argentina. Reviewers say these show a man proud of the killing and committed to an apocalyptic view of race, and that he performed a mild, dutiful role at trial. This is the strongest scholarly objection to Arendt's reading. It leaves open whether 'thoughtlessness' still describes the many people around him, even if it does not describe him well.

images.caption: Hannah Arendt in 1975, the year she died, the political thinker who coined the phrase 'the banality of evil'.
images.credit: Via Wikimedia Commons (author and licence on the file page)

why: The core observation comes from Arendt's first-hand reporting at the 1961 trial and her later philosophical work on thinking, and it remains widely discussed.
Caveat: Stangneth's archival research suggests Eichmann was a committed antisemite who played a part in court, so the idea fits him poorly even if it describes other people's conduct.
Psychologists such as Haslam and Reicher argue that many perpetrators act from conviction, not unthinking obedience.
ideas.try_this: Next time you use 'policy' or 'process' to explain a decision that affects someone, stop and describe it from that person's point of view in two sentences. Does it still sound fine?

ideas.title: Constraints often fuel creativity, not freedom
ideas.idea:
Most of us assume creativity needs freedom: a blank page, no rules, endless options. A good deal of evidence points the other way. A tight constraint rules out the obvious answer, so you are forced to search somewhere new, and the limit gives the search a shape.

Dr Seuss is the usual illustration. In 1960 his publisher, Bennett Cerf, bet him $50 that he could not write an engaging children's book using only 50 different words. The result was Green Eggs and Ham, one of the best-loved children's books ever printed. Seuss had just finished The Cat in the Hat, which used 236 different words, so he was already working inside a tight vocabulary.

The psychologist Karen Haught-Tromp named this the Green Eggs and Ham hypothesis. Her experiments found that people given a constraint wrote rhymes that judges rated as more creative. The point is not that every limit helps, but that a well-chosen one often beats having none.
ideas.deep_dive:
Patricia Stokes, a psychologist, set out the argument in Creativity from Constraints (2005). Looking at painters, writers and designers, she argued that breakthroughs usually come when someone deliberately rules out their own habitual solution, then adds a second constraint that pushes the search towards something unfamiliar. Her account of Monet, for instance, stresses what he chose to avoid as much as what he chose to do. Stokes also separates constraints that open up new possibilities from those that merely push people towards conformity, so the type of limit matters.

The experimental evidence comes from Haught-Tromp (2017, Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts). In two experiments, people wrote a two-line rhyme for a special occasion. In one, they had to include a noun they were given; in the other, they chose their own nouns first and then had to use them. Both studies found that constraints raised the rated creativity of the rhymes. There was also an interaction with the order of the tasks, which the author reads as a carryover effect: practising with a constraint seemed to help later, unconstrained work.

The likely mechanism is that a constraint blocks the first, most available idea. Without one, people tend to settle on the familiar answer. With one, they have to combine things that would not normally go together.

The limits are real. The experiments used a small, artificial task and subjective ratings, not novels or inventions. A constraint that is too severe, or imposed by someone else with no room to reinterpret it, can simply produce frustration. And the 'bet' stories are good ones, but they show a constraint coinciding with success, not causing it.

examples.title: Seuss's fifty-word bet
examples.text: After The Cat in the Hat (1957), which used 236 different words drawn from a list of 348 supplied by an educational publisher, Bennett Cerf wagered Seuss $50 that he could not write a book with only 50 distinct words. Seuss produced Green Eggs and Ham, published in August 1960. Forty-nine of its words are one syllable, and the fiftieth, 'anywhere', has three. Seuss reportedly used notes, charts and checklists to track the vocabulary. Accounts differ on when exactly the bet was made and on whether Cerf ever paid up.

examples.title: Perec writes a novel without 'e'
examples.text: In 1969 the French writer Georges Perec, a member of the Oulipo group of writers and mathematicians, published La Disparition, a novel of roughly 300 pages that never uses the letter e, the commonest letter in French. The plot is built around the constraint: a group searches for a missing friend named Anton Vowl. Gilbert Adair then translated it into English as A Void (1994), also without an e, and it won the Scott Moncrieff Prize. Reviewers treated the English version as a feat in itself, since the translator had to rebuild the puzzle in a new language.

examples.title: Rhymes with a noun to include
examples.text: In Haught-Tromp's experiments, participants wrote two-line rhymes for a special occasion, the sort of verse found in a greeting card. In one study they had to work a given noun into the rhyme; in the other they chose nouns themselves and then had to use them. Judges rated the constrained rhymes as more creative. Because the task is ordinary, you can try it at home: writing a toast or a birthday message becomes easier, and often better, if you first pick three random words and promise to include them. The study also hints that the benefit may carry over to later, unconstrained writing.

why: Evidence: Haught-Tromp's two experiments found a main effect of constraints on rated creativity, and Stokes's book draws the same pattern from case studies of artists and writers.
The experiments use a small, artificial rhyming task with subjective ratings, so they do not prove the effect for novels or inventions.
The famous anecdotes show constraint and success together; they do not prove one caused the other, and too severe or imposed limits can simply frustrate.
ideas.try_this: Pick something you have been stuck on and add one deliberate limit today: half the time, half the words, or one banned obvious option. Notice what you do instead.

ideas.title: When workers are scarce, they gain power
ideas.idea:
When a large share of a population dies, the survivors become scarce, and scarce things gain bargaining power. That is roughly what happened to English workers after the Black Death of 1348–49. Landlords still needed people to plough and harvest, and labourers could ask for more or walk to a better employer.

Parliament tried to stop it. An Ordinance in 1349 and the Statute of Labourers in 1351 ordered wages back to their 1346 level and told able-bodied people to accept work when it was offered. It largely failed. Over the following decades real wages rose, and the old hold of lords over unfree tenants loosened. Yet it was enforced just enough to cause resentment, one strand in the revolt of 1381.

The lesson is not that plague was good for anyone. It is that pay and freedom depend heavily on who needs whom, and that laws pushing against a market's basic pressure tend to leak.
ideas.deep_dive:
The plague reached England in 1348 and killed enough people that land was suddenly plentiful and labour was not. Şevket Pamuk's reconstruction of European wage series finds that real wages roughly doubled in most countries and cities over the century after the first outbreak. A later review by Remi Jedwab, Noel Johnson and Mark Koyama agrees that wages and income per head rose, but adds that the gain lasted in the long run only in some parts of Europe.

The government's answer was to freeze the market. The 1349 Ordinance and the 1351 Statute set maximum wages at 1346 levels, obliged the able-bodied to take work and restricted movement for higher pay. Mark Bailey's recent study of manorial, borough and royal courts shows how the law actually worked, and concludes that it failed. Bailey's earlier work on 1,445 manorial court sessions from six manors found that manorial authorities made few efforts to regulate labour at all.

Historians still argue about timing and cause. Some wage series show real pay falling by about a fifth in the first two years and craftsmen's wages still sliding into the 1360s, with recovery only from the late 1370s, so it was no instant windfall. Gregory Clark finds the rise persisted, with real wages not back at pre-plague levels until the 1600s at the earliest, but sees no sign that agriculture became more efficient. Robert Allen and Pamuk stress a later split: in London and the Low Countries wages stayed well above subsistence, while elsewhere they drifted back, with a clear north-west gap after about 1450.

The limit is that scarcity does not decide everything. In parts of eastern Europe, lords responded to the same shortage by tightening their control over peasants. Law, politics and who holds power decide whether bargaining strength is allowed to bite.

examples.title: The wage freeze that mostly leaked
examples.text: In 1349 and 1351 the English Crown tried to hold pay at 1346 levels and compel people to work. Mark Bailey of the University of East Anglia has studied how this was applied in manorial, borough and royal courts, separating public presentments from private litigation. He argues the laws were more novel than historians once thought, and that they failed. His earlier study of 1,445 manorial court sessions on six manors found that landlords' own courts rarely tried to police wages. The policy was announced by the centre but depended on local employers, who also wanted workers.

image.caption: A later illumination of the death of Wat Tyler at Smithfield in 1381.
image.credit: Via Wikimedia Commons (author and licence on the file page)

examples.title: Essex, 1381: resentment boils over
examples.text: Parliament granted poll taxes in 1377, 1379 and 1380, the last at about a shilling a head. When evasion left a large shortfall, commissioners were sent into the counties in spring 1381, and the revolt is traced to Fobbing in Essex in late May, when one such commissioner arrived. Kent followed and the rebels reached London in mid-June. Wat Tyler was killed at Smithfield on 15 June, and many rebels, including John Ball, were executed afterwards. Historians treat the labour laws as a long-running grievance and the poll tax as the trigger.

examples.title: The US labour market after Covid
examples.text: After the pandemic, American employers struggled to hire. Economists David Autor, Arindrajit Dube and Annie McGrew found that pay for low-wage workers then rose faster than pay for high earners, reversing a decades-long trend. They estimate it offset roughly a quarter to a third of the four-decade rise in wage inequality, depending on the version. Job-to-job moves rose too, especially for young workers without degrees, which they read as employers losing some power over staff. It is a modern, much milder echo of the medieval pattern.

images.credit: Via Wikimedia Commons (author and licence on the file page)

why: Strong support that real wages rose after 1348 across much of Europe (Pamuk, Jedwab, Johnson and Koyama), and that the 1351 Statute failed (Bailey).

Caveats: wages may have dipped first and recovered only from the late 1370s; how much the shortage, rather than peasant resistance or migration, ended serfdom is still debated; eastern Europe went the other way.
ideas.try_this: Think of a job or industry you know where workers are scarce. Who has gained bargaining power, and what rules or contracts are being used to hold it back?

ideas.title: Awe makes the self smaller, and kinder
ideas.idea:
Awe makes us feel smaller, and that may make us kinder. Psychologists define awe as the feeling of meeting something so vast that your usual way of understanding the world cannot quite take it in: a huge tree, a night sky, a person's courage. The interesting part is what it does to the sense of self. In the moment, your own concerns shrink and you feel part of something larger.

In a 2015 study by Paul Piff, Dacher Keltner and colleagues, people who spent a minute looking up at a grove of towering eucalyptus trees then helped a researcher pick up spilled pens more readily than people who had looked at a tall building. The researchers argued that the feeling of a "small self" was part of the reason.

The idea to hold is modest. Awe is a cheap, repeatable way of putting your worries in proportion, and it seems to turn attention outwards.
ideas.deep_dive:
The modern science of awe starts with a 2003 paper by Dacher Keltner and Jonathan Haidt. They argued that awe has two core ingredients: perceived vastness, which can be physical, social or conceptual, and a need for accommodation, meaning the experience does not fit your existing mental structures and you have to stretch them. Other ingredients, such as threat, beauty or moral virtue, change whether awe feels pleasant or unsettling.

Piff and colleagues (2015, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) tested what awe does to the self. Across five studies with around 2,000 participants, awe was triggered by videos, recalled experiences and, in the final study, a minute spent among tall eucalyptus trees. Awe raised generosity and helping, and the authors reported that a diminished sense of self-importance explained part of that effect. Separately, Rudd, Vohs and Aaker (2012, Psychological Science) found that awe made people feel they had more time available, and made them more patient and more willing to volunteer.

Now the caveats. These are mostly short laboratory studies, often with students and with self-reported measures, and the pens test is a single moment of helping, not a change in character. I found no large multi-lab replication. A later three-experiment study with 557 participants found awe reduced aggression and raised prosocial behaviour, but gave only mixed support for the small self being the mechanism. So the safest reading is that awe probably nudges people towards generosity, while exactly why remains open. It is also not a cure for anything; the effects studied are small and brief.

examples.title: Looking up at eucalyptus trees
examples.text: In the final study of Piff and colleagues' 2015 paper, carried out on the University of California, Berkeley campus, participants stood among a grove of tall eucalyptus trees and looked up for a minute. Others stood in the same spot and looked at a tall building. A researcher then appeared to drop a box of pens by accident. Those who had looked at the trees picked up more pens. The team took this as evidence that a brief dose of natural awe can shift behaviour towards helping, even when no one asks for it and nothing is gained.

examples.title: Awe and the feeling of having more time
examples.text: Melanie Rudd, Kathleen Vohs and Jennifer Aaker, reported in 2012 that awe changes how time feels. In the first of three experiments, 63 students watched either a one-minute advert with awe-inspiring scenes or a cheerful parade with confetti. The awe group felt they had more time available. Across the experiments, awe also made people more patient and more willing to give their time to volunteer. The authors argued that awe changes the subjective experience of time, slowing it down.

examples.title: Eight weeks of awe walks
examples.text: At the University of California, San Francisco, Virginia Sturm and colleagues asked older adults to take a weekly 15-minute walk for eight weeks, either with instructions to look for awe in their surroundings or an ordinary walk. In the published analysis of 52 people, median age 75, the awe group reported more daily compassion and gratitude over time. In their selfies, they gradually made themselves smaller in the frame, favouring the landscape, and their smiles grew broader. It is a small study, but the method is something anyone can copy.

images.caption: Eucalyptus regnans, the tallest flowering plant in the world: the kind of towering tree that inspired awe in the Berkeley study (which used a eucalyptus grove).
images.credit: James Aubrey, via Wikimedia Commons (licence on the file page)

why: Piff et al. (2015) ran five studies with about 2,000 people, and Rudd et al. (2012) found related effects, but they are short experiments, often with students.
The small-self explanation is the weakest part: a later 557-person study found only mixed support for it, and I found no large multi-lab replication.
The awe-walk study had 52 older adults, so treat it as encouraging rather than settled.
ideas.try_this: Take ten minutes outdoors today and look for something vast: a big tree, the sky, the sea, a long view. Notice what happens to the thing you were worrying about, and who you feel like talking to afterwards.

ideas.title: Chesterton's fence: know why before removing
ideas.idea:
Before you tear down a rule, a habit or a barrier, find out why someone put it there. That is Chesterton's fence. G. K. Chesterton set it out in his 1929 book The Thing: imagine a fence across a road, and a reformer who sees no use for it and wants it cleared away. The sensible answer is that if he cannot see the point of it, he should not be allowed to remove it. Only someone who has gone off, found out why it was built, and come back can be trusted to say it is no longer needed.

The principle is not a defence of the status quo. If you do discover the reason and it has expired, take the fence down. The target is one specific mistake: treating "I can't see the purpose" as if it meant "there is no purpose". Your ignorance of a reason is a fact about you, not about the fence.
ideas.deep_dive:
The passage comes from Chesterton's chapter "The Drift from Domesticity" in The Thing (1929), where he contrasts two kinds of reformer. The first looks at an institution or law, sees no use in it and wants it gone. The second says, in effect, that if you cannot see the use, you cannot clear it away; go and think, and if you come back and tell him you see its use, he may then allow you to destroy it. The label "Chesterton's fence" came much later and has since been taken up by writers on decision-making, such as Farnam Street.

Why does it work? Rules, habits and structures that survive for a long time have usually met some problem, and the problem is often invisible once the rule is working. A fence that keeps cattle off a road looks pointless in a year when no cattle have strayed, and the absence of cattle is the evidence that it works. Complex systems also depend on parts whose function is not obvious from outside, so removing one is a bet that you understand the whole.

The principle has limits. Investigating costs time, and some fences were built for reasons that were bad, or have long since disappeared. Sometimes the records are lost and nobody can tell you. In that case the question becomes how costly and reversible the removal is: a trial, a staged removal or a reversible change is wiser than a bulldozer. The aim is not to keep everything, but to make the removal an informed decision rather than an act of confidence.

examples.title: China's sparrow campaign, 1958 to 1960
examples.text: In 1958 China's Four Pests campaign set out to wipe out rats, flies, mosquitoes and sparrows, the last for eating grain. Ornithologists warned that sparrows also eat insects, but the campaign went ahead. A University of Chicago working paper (Frank, Wang and colleagues) finds that counties better suited to sparrows lost more rice and wheat after the birds were driven out, and links the effect to roughly two million excess deaths in the Great Famine, which killed an estimated 16.5 to 45 million in all. Sparrows were dropped from the target list in 1960, replaced by bed bugs.

examples.title: Gorsuch's fence in a US Supreme Court dissent
examples.text: On 22 January 2018 the US Supreme Court decided Artis v. District of Columbia by five votes to four, holding that a federal law stops the clock on refiling state-law claims. Justice Neil Gorsuch, joined by Justices Kennedy, Thomas and Alito, dissented. He opened and closed with Chesterton's fence, arguing that a rule whose purpose is not obvious should be understood before it is cleared away, and that the majority was removing a boundary between federal and state power. Whether he was right is a matter of legal debate, but it shows the principle used deliberately as an argument.

examples.title: Knight Capital and the forgotten code
examples.text: On 1 August 2012 the trading firm Knight Capital lost about 440 million dollars in roughly 45 minutes. According to the US Securities and Exchange Commission's account, a new feature had reused a flag that once switched on an old function called Power Peg, which Knight stopped using in 2003 but never deleted. One of eight servers did not receive the new code, so the old function ran and sent millions of unintended orders. The lesson is the mirror image: old parts nobody understands are a hazard whether you remove them or leave them untouched.

why: The principle is a reasoning rule from an essayist, not an experiment; its strength is that it explains many documented failures, such as the sparrow campaign.
The sparrow case has real data behind it (a University of Chicago working paper using agricultural records), though the famine had several causes and the paper's estimate is for sparrow loss alone.
It can be misused to defend anything old. It asks you to look for the reason, not to treat the fence as sacred.
ideas.try_this: Pick one rule, process or habit that annoys you at work or at home. Before you suggest dropping it, spend ten minutes asking the person who has been there longest: what went wrong before this existed?

ideas.title: Fermi estimation: guess in pieces, not in one
ideas.idea:
Fermi estimation means taking a quantity you could never look up, splitting it into parts you can reasonably guess, and multiplying them together. How many piano tuners are there in Chicago? Nobody knows offhand, but you can guess the city's population, how many homes have a piano, how often a piano is tuned and how many a tuner can do in a year. Each guess is rough. The answer is still usually within a factor of two or three.

The trick is that a single wild guess about something unfamiliar can be out by a factor of a hundred. Several small guesses about familiar things are each out by a little, in both directions, and the errors partly cancel when you combine them. You do not get the exact number. You get the right order of magnitude, which is often all you need to decide whether a plan is sensible, an idea is worth pursuing or a claim is absurd.
ideas.deep_dive:
The method is named after the physicist Enrico Fermi, who was known for working out rough answers from almost nothing. The best-known story is his estimate of the yield of the Trinity bomb test in New Mexico on 16 July 1945, described below. In teaching, he is also said to have set students at the University of Chicago the question of how many piano tuners the city had, which is why such puzzles are called Fermi problems.

Why it works comes down to arithmetic. When you multiply several estimated factors, you are adding their logarithms, so one factor that is too high can be offset by another that is too low. If you guess five factors, each wrong by up to a factor of two, the chance that all five miss in the same direction is small. That is why decomposing a problem usually beats guessing the total directly. A second benefit is less obvious: breaking the problem down shows you which assumptions matter most, and where it is worth finding a real figure.

There are limits. The cancelling only works if the errors are roughly independent. If you are biased in the same direction on every factor, they pile up instead. A badly built model, such as leaving out a major part of the problem, is not fixed by clever arithmetic, and some quantities are driven by one factor you cannot know. In the Drake equation, for example, the uncertainty is so large that the output is a range spanning many orders of magnitude. A Fermi estimate is a way to organise what you know and don't know, not a substitute for measurement.

examples.title: Fermi's paper scraps at Trinity
examples.text: At the Trinity test on 16 July 1945, Fermi stood several miles from the explosion. In his own account he dropped small pieces of paper from about six feet before and during the arrival of the blast wave, and measured how far they moved: about 2.5 metres. From that shift he estimated the explosion at ten thousand tons of TNT. The accepted yield is about 21 kilotons, so he was low by about half, but right to within an order of magnitude, from a handful of paper scraps and a quick calculation.

examples.title: Drake's equation at Green Bank, 1961
examples.text: In November 1961 the astronomer Frank Drake opened a small meeting at Green Bank Observatory in West Virginia by writing seven factors on a board: the rate of star formation, the share of stars with planets, habitable planets per system, and the fractions where life, intelligence and detectable technology arise, plus how long a civilisation keeps signalling. It was an agenda, not a result. Only the first factor had any observational basis then. Wikipedia reports the meeting concluded there were probably between 1,000 and 100 million such civilisations in our galaxy, a spread that shows how far one unknown can swamp the rest.

examples.title: Superforecasters break questions down
examples.text: In Superforecasting (2015), Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner describe how the best forecasters in Tetlock's tournaments often used Fermi's approach, which they call Fermi-izing. Their advice is to split a seemingly intractable problem into tractable sub-problems, separating what is knowable from what is not. For the piano-tuner puzzle, that means estimating the number of pianos, how often each is tuned, how long a tuning takes and how many hours a tuner works in a year. The point is to make the guess visible, so it can be checked and argued about.

examples.title: Same puzzle, different answers
examples.text: Classroom write-ups of the Chicago piano-tuner puzzle give different answers because they make different assumptions. One teaching resource from Australia reaches about 34 tuners, another worked version gets about 60, and a third lands near 130. None is wrong as such, since the inputs, such as the city's population and the share of homes with a piano, vary between versions. All of them sit within a factor of about four of each other, which is exactly the accuracy Fermi estimation is designed for. It also shows how much each assumption matters.

images.credit: United States Department of Energy, via Wikimedia Commons (licence on the file page)

images.credit: Via Wikimedia Commons (author and licence on the file page)

why: The Trinity estimate is documented in Fermi's own account and the yield is well established, so this is a real, checkable success, though it came out about half the modern figure.
The error-cancelling effect is well explained mathematically, but it needs independent, unbiased guesses. It is weaker if you are wrong in the same direction every time.
The Drake equation shows the limit: with unknowns spanning many orders of magnitude, a Fermi estimate frames the question but cannot answer it.
ideas.try_this: Estimate something you can check later, such as the number of cafes in your town or the litres of water your household uses in a week. Write each factor down before you look anything up, then compare the result with the real figure.

ideas.title: Why an elephant isn't a hundred thousand mice
ideas.idea: An elephant weighs about 200,000 times what a mouse does, yet it burns only around 9,000 times as much energy. That is Kleiber's law: across mammals, resting metabolic rate rises roughly with body mass raised to the power of three-quarters, not in simple proportion to mass. The consequence is that every kilogram of a large animal runs more slowly than a kilogram of a small one. Gram for gram, a mouse burns something like twenty times the energy of an elephant, so its heart races at several hundred beats a minute while the elephant's ticks over at about thirty. Plot energy use against mass on logarithmic axes and the animals fall along a straight line with a slope of about 0.75, from shrews to whales. Why that number, and whether it is really universal, is still argued over by biologists. The pattern itself is one of the most robust in all of biology.
ideas.deep_dive:
The pattern is named after the biologist Max Kleiber, who worked at what is now the University of California, Davis, and reported in 1932 that metabolic rate scaled with mass to about the three-quarter power. Before that, many biologists expected a two-thirds exponent. The reasoning was geometry: heat is lost through the skin, and surface area grows as the square of length while volume (and so mass) grows as the cube, giving a surface-to-mass relation of two-thirds. Kleiber's data came out closer to three-quarters, and the figure has been repeated in textbooks ever since.

The puzzle was why. In 1997 the physicist Geoffrey West and the ecologists James Brown and Brian Enquist proposed, in Science, that the answer lies in the networks that deliver resources inside a body: arteries, airways and the like. They argued that such networks branch in a space-filling, fractal-like way, end in capillaries of roughly the same size whatever the animal, and are shaped by evolution to minimise the energy needed to pump fluid. A network that does all three delivers supply to the whole body with a three-quarter exponent. The same logic gives related rules: heart rate falls with mass to roughly the power of minus one quarter, and lifespan rises with mass to roughly one quarter.

Those rules explain a famous coincidence. Multiply heart rate by lifespan and most mammals land in the same region, around a billion beats, because the quarter-power terms cancel. Humans are the outlier, with perhaps double that, helped by modern medicine.

Where does it stop applying? The exponent is contested. White and Seymour re-analysed 619 mammal species in 2003 and found 0.69, close to two-thirds. Others reply that the exponent varies between groups, and it does not hold cleanly from one group to another, say from bacteria to insects to mammals. Treat 0.75 as a good rule of thumb, not a law of nature.

examples.title: A billion heartbeats, give or take
examples.text: In 1997 the cardiologist Benjamin Levine's group published, in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, a comparison of resting heart rate and life expectancy across mammals. Multiplying the two gave a lifetime beat count that was, within an order of magnitude, remarkably constant, averaging about 7 x 10^8 and nearer 10^9 after adjustment. A mouse gets there in a couple of years at several hundred beats a minute; a much larger, slower-hearted animal takes decades. The authors read heart rate as a marker of metabolic rate, which is Kleiber's law at work. They also noted that whether slowing the heart could extend human life remained an open question.

examples.title: 619 mammals and a rival exponent
examples.text: In 2003 Craig White and Roger Seymour published a re-analysis of basal metabolic rate in 619 mammal species in PNAS. After correcting for body temperature, whether the animal had finished digesting its last meal, and evolutionary relatedness, they found an exponent of about 0.69, statistically in line with two-thirds rather than three-quarters. They suggested large fermenting herbivores, which take a long time to become fully fasted, had pulled the older figure upwards. This is a good example of how science works around a law: the data got a second look, and the argument over the number is still running.

examples.title: Flatworms that grow and shrink
examples.text: A team led by Albert Thommen and Jochen Rink studied the flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea, which can grow and shrink reversibly across three orders of magnitude in mass. Published in eLife in 2019, their work found Kleiber-like scaling in these animals. It did not come from individual cells slowing down in bigger worms. Instead, larger worms stored more energy per cell, so mass per cell increased. It is evidence that a body can produce the pattern in a way very different from the network story.

why: The three-quarter pattern has been reported for decades across mammals and birds, with Kleiber's 1932 data and many re-analyses since.
The cause is disputed: the 1997 network theory is elegant, but a 2003 PNAS analysis of 619 mammals found an exponent nearer 0.69, and the 2019 flatworm work points to energy storage instead.
It works best inside one group of animals; it should be read as a strong trend with scatter, not an exact law.
ideas.try_this: Next time you see a very small animal, a shrew or a wren, ask what it implies that its heart is racing and it must keep feeding, while a large animal can go for hours without. Then ask which of your own systems (a team, a household, a budget) cost less per unit as they grow, and which cost more.

ideas.title: Moral luck: judged by what happened
ideas.idea:
Two drivers leave the same pub after the same number of drinks, and both swerve onto the footpath. One finds it empty. The other finds a child. We judge the second as a killer and the first as someone who got away with it, though only chance separates them. That is the puzzle of moral luck, named by the philosopher Bernard Williams in 1976 and sharpened by Thomas Nagel in a reply the same year.

The trouble is that we also hold a principle that seems obvious: people should be judged only for what they control. Yet in practice we keep judging people partly by results they did not control. Stanford's Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls this a clash between that Control Principle and our everyday habits of blame. It prompts a question worth asking of any decision, yours or someone else's: if the outcome had gone the other way, would I judge the choice differently?
ideas.deep_dive:
Williams introduced the term in a 1976 paper in the Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society. His best-known case is a loosely fictionalised Gauguin, who leaves his family for Tahiti to paint, without knowing whether he has the talent to be great. Williams argued that what could justify the choice afterwards is success itself, which depends partly on luck. If Gauguin fails, the same decision looks like selfish folly. Nagel's paper appeared in the same volume, and he later expanded it in his 1979 book Mortal Questions.

Nagel then sorted the problem into kinds of luck, which the Stanford entry lists as resultant, circumstantial, constitutive and causal. Resultant luck is luck in how things turn out, and it is the one in the driver story. Circumstantial luck is about the situation you happen to be in. His example is life under the Nazis, where some citizens were tested and failed, while others elsewhere were never tested at all. Constitutive luck is about the temperament you were born with.

The entry sets out the main responses: deny that luck should affect moral assessment, accept that it does, or call the whole idea incoherent. Philosophers still disagree. A useful distinction is between blame and responsibility for consequences. Most people think it right to feel worse about killing someone than about nearly doing so, even when they accept the near-miss driver was just as careless. The puzzle bites hardest when we use outcomes as evidence of quality, which is where psychology has measured the effect directly.

examples.title: Baron and Hershey's outcome bias studies
examples.text: In 1988 Jonathan Baron and John Hershey gave undergraduates descriptions of decisions made under uncertainty, such as a doctor choosing between treatments or a gamble. Everything about the decision was held constant and only the result changed. When the result was good, people rated the thinking as better, the decision-maker as more competent, and were readier to hand them the next decision. Across five studies, the pattern held even though participants were told the decision-maker had the same information. A 2023 replication with 692 online participants found the effect again, including among people who said outcomes should not count.

examples.title: Death sets the sentence for drivers
examples.text: English and Welsh sentencing guidelines show moral luck written into law. Causing death by dangerous driving, in force since July 2023, carries an offence range of 2 to 18 years' custody. For offences after 28 June 2022 the maximum is life. The Sentencing Council's guidance treats death as part of the offence itself. So similar bad driving can land in very different brackets depending on who happened to be in the road. Whether that is justice or luck is the live argument.

examples.title: The nurse who was lucky
examples.text: An NHS England patient-safety presentation by June Woodward describes how health services often react to errors. A nurse whose mistake causes no harm is regarded as lucky, while a colleague who makes the identical mistake and injures a patient is treated as blameworthy. The presentation calls this a flawed system, since outcomes are not fully in anyone's control. Hospitals that follow the Just Culture approach respond to the behaviour, such as carelessness or deliberate risk-taking, rather than the result. The practical aim is that near-misses are reported and learned from, instead of hidden until someone is hurt.

why: The puzzle comes from two heavyweight papers (Williams, Nagel, 1976) and is covered in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; the psychology is measured in Baron and Hershey's five studies and a larger 2023 replication.
Philosophers still disagree on what follows: some say we should blame less by outcome, others that results rightly matter. Outcome bias shows we do it; it does not prove we should not.
Gauguin is fictionalised by Williams himself, so treat it as a thought experiment, not biography.
ideas.try_this: Think of a decision you judged harshly or generously this month because of how it turned out. Ask: if the result had been reversed, what would I have said about the choice itself?
