ideas.title: The commons was not doomed
ideas.idea:
In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published "The Tragedy of the Commons" in Science. His picture was a shared pasture: each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more animal, but the cost of overgrazing is spread across everyone, so every rational herder adds another and the pasture is ruined. For decades the lesson drawn was that shared resources need either private owners or a strong state.

Elinor Ostrom spent her career checking whether this happens in the real world. It often does not. Fishers, farmers and villagers have managed shared forests, pastures, fisheries and irrigation systems for centuries without collapse, by writing their own rules, watching each other and punishing cheats. Hardin had described an open-access free-for-all, not a managed commons. Ostrom's work on exactly this earned her the 2009 Nobel Prize in Economics. The interesting question is no longer whether people can cooperate, but what makes the rules hold.
ideas.deep_dive:
Hardin's essay appeared in Science in 1968 (volume 162, pages 1243 to 1248) and became one of the most cited pieces the journal has published. His model is tidy and, for a resource that really is open to anyone, correct. The weakness is the assumption that herders cannot talk to one another or make rules. Critics, including historians of real commons, pointed out that he showed no actual village where this had happened.

Ostrom's answer, set out in her 1990 book Governing the Commons, was empirical. She began with case studies such as the Swiss village of Törbel and then compared communities that sustained their resources with others that failed. From this she drew eight design principles that recur in the successes: clearly defined boundaries; rules that fit local conditions; users who take part in making the rules; monitoring; graduated sanctions (a small penalty first, heavier ones for repeat offenders); cheap ways to resolve conflicts; recognition by outside authorities of the group's right to organise; and, for larger systems, nested layers of governance.

The mechanism is trust. People keep to a rule when they believe others do too, and that belief depends on visible monitoring and proportionate penalties. Where it stops: the principles were derived by comparing cases, so they are a description of what often works, not a guarantee. Some of her showpiece cases have been questioned by later researchers, and commons fail when outsiders can walk in, when groups are too large or too unequal, or when monitoring is impossible. Global problems such as the climate have no boundary or shared community, which is why they are so much harder.

examples.title: Törbel's Alpine pasture rules
examples.text: Törbel, a village in the Swiss canton of Valais, has shared its high summer pasture, forest and irrigation for centuries. Robert Netting studied it, and Ostrom made it a founding case. The key rule, as the sources give it, is that nobody may send more cows to the alp than they can feed through the winter on their own hay, which stops anyone loading the common pasture with extra animals. Only village members have rights, and everyone can see how many cattle each member sends, so breaches are noticed and penalised. Formal articles of association date from 1483. Later work on the Grisons region questions how far Netting's account generalises.

examples.title: Maine's lobster harbour gangs
examples.text: In Maine a state licence lets you fish, but in practice you also need to be accepted by the local harbour gang, an informal group of as few as eight and rarely more than fifty boats that holds a territory. The anthropologist James Acheson documented this in The Lobster Gangs of Maine (1988). Intruders get verbal warnings first; if they persist, their traps may be cut, which is illegal and risky. Fishers also notch the tails of egg-bearing females and return them to the sea, a conservation norm that spread informally from the mid twentieth century. Acheson linked these rules to Maine's healthy catches, though the system is eroding offshore.

examples.title: Valencia's farmers' water court
examples.text: Every Thursday at noon, at the Apostles' Door of Valencia Cathedral, a court of elected farmers settles disputes over irrigation water drawn from the River Turia. Each of the irrigation communities sends a representative (the síndic), and the proceedings are public and oral, in Valencian and judgments are given on the spot. Its origins are traced to at least the tenth century, though that is uncertain. UNESCO added it, together with the Council of Wise Men of Murcia, to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2009,, the year Ostrom won her Nobel.

Hardin's model is right for genuinely open-access resources; his error was treating every shared resource as one.
Limits: the design principles were induced from cases and some cases, such as Törbel, have been contested. Global commons like the climate lack a bounded community.
ideas.try_this: Pick one shared resource in your life (a kitchen, a shared drive, a local green space). Does it have clear boundaries, visible monitoring and a mild first penalty? Change one of those and see whether behaviour shifts.

ideas.title: When people fail, blame the design
ideas.idea: When someone makes a mistake with a door, a stove or a control panel, the instinct is to call it human error. Don Norman, the cognitive scientist and designer, argued the opposite in The Design of Everyday Things: if a sensible person keeps getting it wrong, the fault usually lies with the design. A door with an identical handle on both sides gives no clue whether to push or pull, so the person who pushes a pull door has done nothing foolish. They have been misled. The practical consequence is a different question. Instead of asking who slipped, ask what the design let them believe, what it failed to show, and why one slip could do so much damage. People are predictably imperfect, so good systems are built to expect errors, make the right action obvious, and make the wrong one hard, reversible or visible straight away.
ideas.deep_dive:
Norman's book first appeared in 1988 as The Psychology of Everyday Things and was later retitled and, in 2013, revised and expanded. Its starting point is that people act on what a design tells them. He distinguishes discoverability (can you work out what actions are possible?) from understanding (do you know what they mean?). In the revised edition he introduced the word signifier for the visible cue that tells you where an action should happen: a flat plate says push, a handle says pull. The doors that break this rule became known as Norman doors, a name he has said he accepts with some dismay and secret pride.

The larger argument is about error. Norman's chapter on the subject is called "Human Error? No, Bad Design". Slips, such as pressing the wrong switch, and mistakes, such as misreading the situation, are normal products of attention and memory. If your design only works when nobody is ever tired, rushed or distracted, it does not work. So designers should make state visible, provide feedback, keep dangerous actions apart from harmless ones, and allow recovery.

This changes how investigations run. Asking "why did the person do that?" tends to stop at a name. Asking "why did that action make sense at the time?" leads back to labels, layouts, procedures and incentives. Note the limits. Some failures do involve negligence or deliberate rule-breaking, and not every accident has a design culprit. The claim is narrower and more useful: when a mistake is easy to make and repeated by different people, treat the person as the symptom, not the cause.

examples.title: Three Mile Island's misleading indicator light
examples.text: On 28 March 1979 a relief valve on the reactor at Three Mile Island, Pennsylvania, stuck open and coolant drained away. The control-room light for that valve showed only that the signal to close it had been sent, not that the valve had actually closed. Operators who trusted the light did not realise the loss of coolant was continuing, and it ran on for over two hours. The President's Commission, chaired by John Kemeny, also listed poor training, unclear procedures and control-room design as contributing causes. It did not stop at "operator error".

examples.title: Hawaii's false missile alert, 2018
examples.text: At 8:08 a.m. on 13 January 2018, a ballistic missile alert went to phones across Hawaii and was not corrected for 38 minutes. The state first blamed a wrong menu choice. The Federal Communications Commission found something more systemic: the employee believed a drill was real, because the drill recording wrongly included the words "This is not a drill". Nobody else had to confirm a live alert, and there was no ready procedure for correcting a false one. The FCC concluded the cause was human error plus inadequate safeguards, and recommended two-person validation and keeping test and live alerts apart in the software.

examples.title: The push-pull door in everyday life
examples.text: A Norman door is any door whose design gives the wrong signal about whether to push, pull or slide, often because the same handle is fitted on both sides. In 2016 Roman Mars of 99% Invisible and Joe Posner of Vox interviewed Norman about them, and the term spread well beyond design circles. Norman has written that he feels dismay and secret pride that badly designed doors are called Norman doors. The cheap fix works at the level of signifiers: a flat plate where you push, a handle where you pull, so nobody needs a sign saying which.

why: The core argument is a long-standing principle in human factors, backed by Norman's book and by official inquiries into Three Mile Island and the 2018 Hawaii alert.

The Hawaii case is messier than the first story: the FCC found a misunderstood drill, not a simple wrong click, and officials' released screenshots of the interface were disputed. The lesson holds, but the detail needs care.
Limit: design is rarely the only cause. Training, procedures and individual choices matter too, and genuine negligence exists.
ideas.try_this: Pick one thing at home or work that people keep getting wrong (a form, a door, a shared spreadsheet). Instead of reminding people to be careful, change one thing so the wrong action is harder or the right one is obvious.

ideas.title: The bystander effect is weaker than the myth
ideas.idea: Most of us learned that a crowd makes people less likely to help: the more witnesses, the less anyone acts. The story behind it, that 38 neighbours watched Kitty Genovese die in New York in 1964 and did nothing, turns out to be largely false. And the effect, though real in some laboratory settings, shrinks sharply when a situation is clearly dangerous. When researchers watched what actually happened in 219 real conflicts caught on street cameras in three countries, someone intervened in about 91 per cent of them, and victims were more, not less, likely to get help as the crowd grew. The sensible conclusion is not that people never freeze. It is that help is the usual response in real emergencies, and that the old parable has been scaring us about each other for sixty years without good reason.
ideas.deep_dive:
The textbook version begins in March 1964, when a young woman, Kitty Genovese, was attacked and killed in Kew Gardens, Queens. A New York Times story claimed that 38 witnesses had watched and none had called for help. Two psychologists in New York, Bibb Latané and John Darley, took up the question, and their laboratory experiments through the late 1960s showed that people were often slower to act when others were present. The finding was named the bystander effect and was taught for decades.

In 2007 Rachel Manning, Mark Levine and Alan Collins went back to the trial records and police files for American Psychologist. They found no evidence for 38 witnesses, or that those who knew something was wrong had seen the attack, or that they stayed inactive. Prosecutor Charles Skoller later said only about half a dozen could be used, and the fatal attack took place inside a building, out of sight. In 2016 the Times itself called its original reporting flawed.

The laboratory effect is a separate matter. In 2011 Peter Fischer and colleagues pooled 105 effect sizes from over 7,700 participants in Psychological Bulletin. They found a real overall effect (g = -0.35), but it weakened where a situation was seen as dangerous, where a perpetrator was present, and where helping would carry a physical cost.

The third step came from cameras. Richard Philpot and colleagues studied 219 aggressive incidents captured on CCTV, and found intervention in 91 per cent.

The limits: the footage came from city centres, so it excludes some of the most violent gang-related areas, and a camera cannot tell you what people were thinking. Crowds can still freeze in ambiguous situations. The better lesson is narrower: when something is clearly wrong, people usually act.

examples.title: What really happened on Austin Street
examples.text: The 38-witness story came from a New York Times report on the killing of Kitty Genovese in Kew Gardens, Queens, in 1964. In 2007 Manning, Levine and Collins reviewed the trial and police records and found no support for it. They found no evidence of 38 witnesses who saw the attack and did nothing. One neighbour shouted at the attacker, who briefly broke off. The fatal assault then happened inside a building where witnesses could not see. In 2016 the Times called its own early reporting flawed. The parable lasted because it was a tidy story.

examples.title: 219 fights, filmed by accident
examples.text: Richard Philpot and colleagues at Lancaster University, with researchers from Copenhagen and the Netherlands, analysed 219 arguments and assaults recorded on public CCTV in inner-city Amsterdam, Lancaster and Cape Town. In 91 per cent, at least one bystander intervened, by calming the aggressor, blocking or pulling them away, or comforting the victim. The odds of help rose by about 10 per cent with each extra bystander. Rates did not differ significantly between the three cities, though Cape Town is seen as less safe. Philpot argued more people simply means a bigger pool of potential helpers.

examples.title: A meta-analysis that found a hidden catch
examples.text: In 2011 Peter Fischer and eight co-authors pooled 105 effect sizes from over 7,700 participants across decades of bystander experiments, published in Psychological Bulletin. Overall, people were slightly less likely to help when others were present (g = -0.35). But the effect weakened when the situation was seen as dangerous, when the perpetrator was present, or when helping carried a physical cost. The authors explained this with the arousal-cost-reward model: dangerous emergencies are recognised faster as real emergencies, so the usual confusion about whether anything is wrong fades.

why: Three separate lines of evidence agree: the 2007 archival review of the Genovese case, the 2011 meta-analysis of 105 effect sizes, and the CCTV study of 219 real incidents.
The laboratory effect is real but modest, and it shrinks in dangerous emergencies.
Caveat: the CCTV footage is from city centres and shows what people did, not why, and ambiguous situations can still leave people hesitating.
ideas.try_this: Next time you are in a crowd and something seems off, ask yourself: what would I do if I knew it was an emergency? Then act on that, because others are probably waiting for someone to move first.

ideas.title: We underestimate how much thanks means
ideas.idea:
Most of us have someone we mean to thank properly and never do. The reasons sound sensible: it will be awkward, I will not say it well, they know already. In 2018 the psychologists Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley tested those worries in Psychological Science. People wrote a gratitude letter to someone who had made a difference to them, predicted how the reader would feel, and then the researchers found out how the readers really felt.

The writers got it wrong in a consistent direction. They underestimated how surprised and how positive the recipients would be, and they overestimated how awkward the recipients would feel. Writers fretted about how well they had put things. Recipients mostly noticed the warmth of being thought of.

The lesson is narrower than a cure-all: when your instinct says a thank-you will land flat, that instinct is probably biased, and the cost of testing it is a few minutes.
ideas.deep_dive:
The paper is "Undervaluing Gratitude: Expressers Misunderstand the Consequences of Showing Appreciation", Kumar and Epley, Psychological Science, 2018. Across several experiments (coverage varies between three and four) participants wrote a letter to someone who had affected their life in a meaningful way. Before sending, writers predicted how recipients would feel: how surprised, how positive, how awkward. The researchers then contacted the recipients and asked them.

The gap was consistent. Recipients were more surprised that the writer was grateful, and more surprised by the reasons, than writers expected. They felt more positive than predicted, and less awkward. The authors' explanation is a difference in perspective. Writers concentrate on competence: is this well written, will I sound clumsy? Recipients concentrate on warmth and intent: someone bothered. Writers may also assume the other person already knows how they feel, so a letter seems to add little. According to the British Psychological Society's digest, the misjudgment also shaped willingness to send: people were least inclined to write to those they thought would benefit least.

There are limits. The sample consisted of letters people chose to write about relationships that mattered, so it does not tell us about formulaic thanks, or about thanks that is insincere. Coverage notes that a gesture seen as disingenuous could land very differently. The study also measures how recipients felt at a moment, not lasting effects on a relationship. Separate work on gratitude letters found the happiness boost for writers had faded by six months, so the benefit should not be oversold.

examples.title: The letter-writing experiments themselves
examples.text: In Kumar and Epley's experiments, participants wrote to someone they felt they had never adequately thanked. Writers then forecast how surprised and happy the recipient would be and how awkward. When the recipients were contacted, the forecasts were off in every experiment: recipients were more surprised and more positive than expected and less awkward. Writers were also unduly worried about expressing gratitude skilfully, while recipients responded simply to the warmth of the gesture. The paper's own summary is that expressing gratitude may not buy everything, but it may buy more than people expect.

examples.title: Couples under-read each other's thanks
examples.text: A study of romantic relationships, indexed on PubMed Central, used an accuracy and bias approach to compare how much gratitude partners felt with how much the other person perceived. Perceivers generally underestimated their partner's gratitude, and lower perceived gratitude went with lower relationship satisfaction for the perceiver. It is a different setting from letters, but it points the same way: the thanks we feel often goes unnoticed, so saying it aloud is not redundant. Familiarity does not guarantee the message has landed.

examples.title: Seligman's gratitude visit
examples.text: In a 2005 American Psychologist study, Martin Seligman and colleagues asked internet volunteers in one condition to write a letter of gratitude and deliver it in person within a week. Summaries by Berkeley's Greater Good in Action report that this exercise gave the biggest boost to happiness a month later of the exercises tested, with participants also less depressed. By six months, happiness had returned to where it started. So the benefit to the writer is real but short-lived, and the recipient's side was not what the study measured.

why: The core finding comes from a peer-reviewed paper (Kumar and Epley, 2018) and is reported consistently by the University of Chicago, Chicago Booth, the British Psychological Society and the Association for Psychological Science.

Caveat: the participants wrote to people who mattered and were willing to take part, so it says little about forced, formulaic or insincere thanks, and sources disagree on whether there were three or four experiments.
ideas.try_this: Pick one person you have meant to thank properly. Write three or four sentences saying what they did and what difference it made, and send it today before you can talk yourself out of it.

ideas.title: Desire paths: let users show you the route
ideas.idea: A desire path is the dirt track worn across a lawn by people who ignored the pavement and took the shortest or easiest way. Planners often treat it as a nuisance, but it is also free research: a map of what people actually want, drawn by the people who matter, with no survey and no bias. The idea for designers is to watch behaviour before you commit to a layout. Let people use the space, see where the grass wears away, then build the formal route along it. The same logic applies to software and organisations. When users invent workarounds, copy and paste a code, or add a convention the system never planned for, they are marking a desire path. The sensible response is usually to learn from it, not to scold people for leaving the official route.
ideas.deep_dive:
The phrase is often credited to the French philosopher Gaston Bachelard, who is said to have written of les chemins du desir in The Poetics of Space. Be wary of that. A library-science paper notes the attribution is widely repeated, but that the book itself makes no explicit mention of desire lines. Treat the origin of the term as unsettled; the phenomenon is not. Other names include elephant paths, cow paths and desire lines.

The mechanism is simple. A route is chosen by cost: time, effort, comfort, the mud on a wet day. Planners usually draw the plan from above and from the entrances of buildings, while walkers decide from the ground, one step at a time. Each person who cuts a corner makes the next person's choice slightly easier, because the grass is already flattened. Within weeks, a faint track becomes a visible line. In effect, many individual decisions combine into a vote.

That is why some campuses deliberately waited. Others plan holistically and try to get the layout right first time; a University of Wisconsin-Madison planner has described the aim as a balance between paving everything and keeping green space.

The limits matter. A desire path shows what is convenient, not necessarily what is good. It can cut through flower beds, erode slopes, create mud, or be unusable for someone in a wheelchair or with a pram, and some critics argue they exclude people. Treat them as evidence to weigh, not as an instruction. The best use is as a first question: why did so many people reject the route we gave them?

examples.title: Michigan State left the grass unpaved
examples.text: Michigan State University says some informal paths were created by students around its founding in 1855 and later shaped the sidewalk network still used on campus. A design write-up on Pop-Up City describes the early public space as grass only, with footpaths deliberately missing, so that students would pick the shortest routes between buildings; the paths were then asphalted and formalised roughly a year later. A University of Wisconsin-Madison news story uses MSU as the contrast to its own practice of planning pathways in advance. The detail is sourced to university material and a design blog, not to the original plans.

examples.title: Virginia Tech paved the worn Drillfield tracks
examples.text: In summer 2014 Virginia Tech paved three dirt paths that students had worn across the Drillfield, its central lawn. The university said the routes had evolved from use rather than from any plan, and that they were muddy and tracked dirt into buildings. The new asphalt strips were five feet wide, against twelve feet for the older paths. Officials called the work a temporary fix while they sought a long-term design, and in 2015 they laid test paths in 13 materials. Reaction was mixed: some students wanted the green space kept for sport, others welcomed dry routes.

examples.title: Twitter learned hashtags from its users
examples.text: Early Twitter had no way to group posts by topic. On 23 August 2007 Chris Messina, a user and designer, proposed using the # sign, and a few days later set out a fuller proposal. Reports say Twitter's founders thought it too nerdy to catch on. Users adopted it anyway, notably for the 2007 San Diego wildfires, and in 2009 Twitter began linking hashtags to search. It is the digital version of the same story: a route worn by users, later paved by the company.

Evidence is mostly case-based, not experimental. Some campus tales, such as a 1914 balloon survey of snow tracks, rest on a single blog and are left out here.
Limit: a worn path shows convenience, not safety, access or environmental cost, so weigh it against other needs.
ideas.try_this: Find one shortcut or workaround people keep using around you: a worn corner, a spreadsheet hack, a message format. Ask what the official route fails to offer, and whether you could build the formal version along it.

ideas.title: Clair Patterson and the lead in everything
ideas.idea:
The geochemist Clair Patterson set out to answer a simple question: how old is the Earth? To do it he had to count tiny amounts of lead in meteorites, and his samples kept coming out contaminated. Chasing the contamination turned a pure-science project into one of the great public health stories of the twentieth century.

In 1956 he published an age for the Earth of about 4.55 billion years, a figure that has barely moved since. Then he asked where all the stray lead had come from. His answer was that lead was not a trace natural element in the modern environment but a pervasive industrial pollutant, with leaded petrol a leading source. He spent decades arguing this against an industry that had paid for much of the opposing science. The idea: the clean measurement you need for one question can reveal a far bigger problem you were not looking for, and a comfortable consensus can rest on contaminated data.
ideas.deep_dive:
Patterson's age of the Earth came from lead isotopes in the Canyon Diablo meteorite, the iron meteorite associated with Meteor Crater in Arizona. Meteorites are leftovers from the formation of the solar system, so their lead records how much radioactive decay of uranium has happened since. Comparing isotope ratios gave a date. His 1956 paper put the Earth at about 4.55 billion years, with an uncertainty of around 70 million, far more accurate than earlier estimates.

The hard part was contamination. To measure so few atoms he built one of the first clean rooms, filtering the air, acid-washing equipment and distilling his reagents. Even so, he found lead in glassware, tap water, dust and paint. Working with Mitsunobu Tatsumoto, he showed in 1963 that deep ocean water held several times less lead than surface water (the National Academies biography gives 3 to 10 times), suggesting modern human sources. In 1965 he published a long paper on contaminated and natural lead environments, arguing that the northern hemisphere's atmosphere held roughly a thousand times its natural lead and that lead additives in petrol should be removed.

The opposing view was championed by Robert Kehoe, who had been hired in 1924 to look into health problems of tetraethyl lead production and directed a laboratory funded by Ethyl, General Motors and DuPont. Kehoe held that low-level lead was a normal part of the human environment. Patterson's central point was that industry should not be the only judge of its own product's safety. Where it stops: Patterson's figures differ between sources, and the proof of harm to children came later, from other researchers.

examples.title: Dating the Earth from a meteorite
examples.text: In the early 1950s at Caltech, Patterson analysed lead from the Canyon Diablo meteorite, fragments of which were found around Meteor Crater in Arizona. He had to count lead atoms in minute samples and separate four isotopes of lead, which meant building a contamination-free laboratory himself. He finished the analysis in 1953 and published the age of about 4.55 billion years in 1956. Estimates before this had been much less precise. The figure has stood for nearly seventy years, and it is the reason the Earth's age is quoted with such confidence today.

image.caption: A specimen of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, the iron meteorite Patterson used to date the Earth.
image.credit: Geoffrey Notkin / CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

examples.title: Industry pushback and the Senate hearing
examples.text: When Patterson's 1965 paper appeared, the American Petroleum Institute replied in September that his findings might be of academic interest but had no real bearing on public health. Funding from oil companies for his research dried up; in his own oral history he said they stopped his work after he blamed leaded petrol. In 1966 he and Kehoe testified before a US Senate subcommittee chaired by Edmund Muskie. Kehoe argued that his own laboratory was the main source of reliable information on lead exposure, while Patterson criticised public health agencies for relying on industry-linked research.

examples.title: What happened to the lead in children
examples.text: The United States began cutting lead in petrol in 1973, with a gradual phase-down, and the Clean Air Act ban on leaded petrol for road vehicles took full effect on 1 January 1996. Our World in Data reports that the average blood lead of American children aged one to five was 15 micrograms per decilitre in 1978; by 2016 the median was 0.7, a fall of 95 per cent, with petrol the biggest single cause of the drop. Globally, the UN announced in August 2021 that Algeria had used its last stocks, ending leaded petrol worldwide; UNEP estimated that this prevents 1.2 million premature deaths a year.

images.caption: A specimen of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, the iron meteorite Patterson used to date the Earth.
images.credit: Geoffrey Notkin / CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

why: The 4.55 billion year age is one of the most robust results in earth science, and the lead-in-the-environment findings were confirmed by later studies of ice, water and blood lead that tracked the petrol phase-out.
Evidence on harm: blood lead fell steeply as leaded petrol was withdrawn, in the US and elsewhere.
Caveat: popular retellings simplify. Patterson did not act alone, and sources disagree on some figures, such as how much lead was in polar ice or the exact pressure applied to him.
ideas.try_this: Think of a number or fact you treat as a natural baseline (normal cholesterol, normal traffic fumes, a normal level of anything). Who measured it, and could the measurement itself have been contaminated by the thing it is meant to be free of?
